title: HP Protein Folding
origin: In 1985, Ken Dill introduced the HP model as the simplest non-trivial model of protein folding. Proteins are reduced to chains of two types of amino acids: H (hydrophobic, water-avoiding) and P (polar, water-loving). The chain must fold onto a lattice without crossing itself, and the goal is to maximize contacts between H residues — mimicking the hydrophobic collapse that drives real protein folding. Despite its simplicity, finding the optimal fold was proven NP-hard in 1998. Standard benchmark sequences of length 48 to 100 have best-known folds from the 1990s and 2000s that have never been proven optimal. Beating any of these records would be a publishable result.
instance: Choose a benchmark sequence from the records table. Each sequence is a string of H and P characters. Find a self-avoiding walk on the 2D square lattice (one lattice point per residue, consecutive residues on adjacent points, no two residues on the same point) that maximizes H-H contacts. A contact is a pair of H residues that are adjacent on the lattice but not consecutive in the sequence. Submit the lattice coordinates of each residue.

scoring.summary: Each submission is scored by the number of H-H topological contacts in the fold. Higher is better. Beat the current record to claim a spot on the leaderboard.

metrics.name: H-H contacts
metrics.description: The number of non-sequential H-H pairs that are lattice-adjacent. This is the primary score. Higher is better (lower energy).

metrics.name: New record
metrics.description: If your contact count strictly exceeds the current best known for that sequence, you have a new record.

metrics.name: Compactness (tiebreaker)
metrics.description: For equal contact counts, the fold with smaller radius of gyration (tighter packing) ranks higher.

scoring.note: Sequences S1-S4 have proven optimal folds. Sequences S5-S10 have best-known folds that may be suboptimal — these are the real targets. Any valid self-avoiding fold is accepted and scored.

warmup.title: Warm-up: 6-residue all-H chain
warmup.body: Fold the sequence HHHHHH on a 2D square lattice. Since every residue is H, any non-sequential lattice adjacency is a contact. One optimal fold forms a 2x3 snake: (0,0), (1,0), (1,1), (0,1), (0,2), (1,2). This achieves 2 H-H contacts: positions 0-3 (via (0,0)-(0,1) adjacency) and positions 2-5 (via (1,1)-(1,2) adjacency). Verify: check each pair (i,j) with |i-j| > 1, both H, Manhattan distance 1 between their coordinates. The maximum for HHHHHH on a 2D lattice is 2 contacts.

verification: For each submission: (1) Check coords length matches sequence length, (2) Check all coordinates are unique (self-avoidance), (3) Check consecutive residues are lattice-adjacent (Manhattan distance = 1), (4) Count H-H contacts: pairs (i, j) where |i-j| > 1, both sequence[i] and sequence[j] are H, and coords are lattice-adjacent. Pure integer arithmetic, runs in microseconds.

bounds.label: Complexity
bounds.name: NP-hard
bounds.formula: Proven NP-complete in 3D by Berger & Leighton (1998) and in 2D by Crescenzi et al. (1998). No polynomial-time algorithm is known or expected.

bounds.label: Search space
bounds.name: Exponential
bounds.formula: ~mu^n self-avoiding walks (mu ≈ 2.638 for the 2D square lattice). For n=100: approximately 10^42 conformations.

bounds.label: Upper bound
bounds.name: Contacts <= H*(H-1)/2
bounds.formula: Each H residue has at most 4 lattice neighbors (2D) minus the 1-2 occupied by chain neighbors. The packing limit depends on H-density and chain topology.

bounds.label: Proven optima
bounds.name: Known for benchmark sequences up to length 36
bounds.formula: Exhaustive search and branch-and-bound have confirmed optimal values for the standard benchmark sequences S1-S4 (lengths 20-36). Beyond that, only heuristic best-known values exist.

leaderboard.note: Standard benchmark sequences for 2D HP lattice folding. Sources: Unger & Moult (1993), Yue & Dill (1995), various metaheuristic papers. Records for S5-S10 are best-known, not proven optimal.

rows.note: Open — Wust & Landau (2012) found putative ground state
Open — longest standard benchmark. Putative ground state -50 from Wang-Landau sampling (Wust & Landau, 2012)

suggestedApproach.title: Verify the warm-up
suggestedApproach.body: Fold the 6-residue all-H chain on paper or in code. Verify the 2x3 snake achieves 2 contacts by checking all pairs (i,j) with |i-j|>1 for lattice adjacency. Then try the first benchmark sequence S1 (length 20) to build intuition for mixed H/P chains.

suggestedApproach.title: Pull moves for Monte Carlo
suggestedApproach.body: Standard single-residue moves get stuck in local minima. Use pull moves (Lesh et al., 2003): grab a residue and pull the chain to a new position while maintaining connectivity. This allows large conformational changes.

suggestedApproach.title: Simulated annealing with restarts
suggestedApproach.body: Energy = -(H-H contacts). Start hot (accept bad moves), cool slowly. Run many independent starts and keep the best. Most record-setting results used this approach.

suggestedApproach.title: Genetic algorithm
suggestedApproach.body: Encode folds as sequences of relative moves (L, R, S for left, right, straight). Crossover partial folds. Select for high contact count. Multi-population with migration often helps.

suggestedApproach.title: Target the long sequences
suggestedApproach.body: S9 (length 85) and S10 (length 100) have the least attention and the most room for improvement. These are the highest-value targets.

suggestedApproach.title: Reinforcement learning
suggestedApproach.body: Train an RL agent to place residues one at a time on the lattice, rewarding H-H contacts. The state space is manageable for lengths up to 100.

agentPrompt: I want you to find optimal or near-optimal folds for HP protein sequences on a 2D square lattice. Each sequence is a string of H (hydrophobic) and P (polar) characters. Place each residue on a unique point of the integer lattice such that consecutive residues are adjacent (Manhattan distance 1). Maximize H-H contacts: pairs of H residues that are lattice-adjacent but not sequence-adjacent. Start with sequence S5 (length 48): PPHPPHHPPHHPPPPPHHHHHHHHHHPPPPPPHHPPHHPPHPPHHHHH. The current record is 23 contacts. Use simulated annealing with pull moves: initialize a random self-avoiding walk, then repeatedly select a random residue and attempt to pull it to a new lattice position while maintaining chain connectivity. Accept moves that increase contacts, and occasionally accept worse moves (Metropolis criterion) to escape local minima. Cool the temperature slowly over millions of steps. Run multiple independent trials and report the best fold found as a JSON array of [x, y] coordinates.
